meaning: 'Womb, source' — the feminine principle, the origin from which all creation flows

The feminine principle, the origin — paired with the liṅga in Śaiva worship.

pronunciation.note: The word means womb, source, and place of origin — the feminine as the container of creation.

domains.title: The Womb, the Feminine Principle
domains.subtitle: The Source from Which All Creation Flows
domains.lead: Yoni is the source: the womb, the origin-place, the feminine principle that the Śaiva tradition pairs with the liṅga as the two-in-one of all generation. In philosophy it names the material cause — prakṛti, the matrix from which the differentiated world flows; in ritual it is the altar’s base, the goddess’s body, and the cosmic ground on which the god stands.

cards.name: The Liṅga-Yoni
cards.desc: The Śaiva aniconic pair: the standing mark in the flowing base — creation and its ground, united.

cards.name: The Material Cause
cards.desc: In Sāṃkhya-Yoga, prakṛti the yoni is the womb of the world — all effects pre-exist in their cause.

cards.name: The Goddess’s Body
cards.desc: In the Śākta traditions the yoni is the goddess herself — the pīṭha, the sacred seat of power.

cards.name: The Ritual Base
cards.desc: Every Śaiva altar’s foundation is the yoni-shaped basin, catching the libation that feeds the god.

mythology.lead: The yoni’s mythology is the Śaiva theology of the pair: the god and his power, the liṅga and its base, the still and the flowing. Its narratives are the Goddess-traditions’ own — Satī’s sacrifice, the dismembered pīṭhas, and the tantric ritual in which the base is the goddess’s body receiving the god’s libation. The word itself is the doctrine: the womb as the world’s first fact.

myths.title: The Endless Pillar and Its Base
myths.text: The tradition’s founding image: the endless pillar of fire — the liṅga without top or bottom — that humbled Brahmā and Vishnu, standing in the yoni-base as the ground of the ground. The Purāṇa’s theology is exact: the mark is the god, the base is his power, and worship of the one without the other is incomplete.

myths.title: The Dismembered Seat
myths.text: When Satī self-immolated at her father’s insult, Śiva wandered the world with her corpse, and the pieces fell as the śakti-pīṭhas — each a seat of the goddess’s power, each in some tellings marked by the yoni. The tantric pilgrimages map the goddess’s body onto the subcontinent: the womb as sacred geography.

myths.title: The Rite of the Base
myths.text: In the tantric pūjā the yoni-basin receives the libations poured over the liṅga, channelling the offering to the goddess below. The ritual grammar is the theology in action: creation as the union of the standing god and the flowing ground, generation as worship.

myths.title: The Matrix of Causes
myths.text: The Sāṃkhya makes yoni technical: prakṛti, the material cause, is the womb in which all effects pre-exist — the tree in the seed, the world in the matrix. The doctrine of satkāryavāda, ‘the effect pre-exists in the cause’, is the philosophy of the yoni stated as metaphysics.

lore.syncretism: The yoni-liṅga pair absorbed every Indian polarity — puruṣa and prakṛti, god and goddess, stillness and flow — into a single aniconic form. The tantric traditions made it explicit worship; the Puranic made it respectable; and the modern world received it as scandal and symbol at once, usually without the theology.
lore.culturalLegacy: The liṅga-yoni is Hinduism’s most reproduced and least understood image — the tourist’s puzzle and the theologian’s précis. ‘Yoni’ entered English in the nineteenth century as a learned word; and the goddess’s-seats (śakti-pīṭhas) remain the subcontinent’s most charged pilgrimage geography.
lore.extendedMeditation: Yoni: the source-word, restored in plain letters that offer no euphemism and need none. The lexicon holds it as the tradition does — beside the liṅga, as the ground holds the standing thing. Two syllables, the world’s first fact.
lore.archaeology: The yoni’s monuments are the oldest Śaiva remains: the Gupta liṅgas with their carved bases, the Gudimallam ithyphallic Śiva, and the aniconic aniconism of every village shrine’s stone pair. The pīṭha-stones of Kāmākhyā are its most charged site.
lore.cult: The daily liṅga-pūjā is its liturgy — the pouring, the catching, the feeding of the ground. The menstruation-temples of the goddess-traditions (Kāmākhyā above all) keep its most esoteric calendar.
lore.iconography: The liṅga rising from the yoni-basin, the channel of the libation cut into the base; or the goddess’s body as the seat. Its icon is the union: never the one without the other.
lore.reception: Religious studies treats the pair as the classic case of aniconic representation carrying full theology; and the modern West’s reception — oscillating between snigger and reverence — is itself a chapter in the study of how cultures misread what they have no grammar for.
